Now, if something has been pulled out of the notebook, I can't reconstruct it. I can't put in another page to fill in the gap. So there are various lists of weapons issued and lists of everything, but quite obviously the notebook was kept from 1992, because the information dates from 1992 onwards, who was killed in 1992, who was wounded in 1992, and so on. So if the notebook was kept by somebody who wasn't very intelligent and wasn't very well educated, but had nice handwriting, you can't hold it against him or against the notebook. It's one platoon; it's not a brigade or a division, it's just a platoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, that's your testimony. We would need to hear a witness here who will testify to what you are saying. How can we work this out? You're not a witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madame Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have understood what the issue hinges on. Put your question to the witness, and we will assess the outcome of this in line --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... during the examination-in-chief, and he repeated that today, that those alleged 20 Chetniks who came with Vaske from Knin and stayed in Ilijas, and that they left Ilijas at the end of war, that's what he said. So they must have been there throughout. Now, the most important point in this whole notebook is can we find the name of a person who is not from Ilijas and the surrounding parts, and if you can, whether it's one or two names or can you find twenty names of people who are not from there? And my question could be, although I didn't mean to dwell on this for that long because we'll have more evidence about Ilijas - I have photocopies of military booklets here and some other documents as well - Vasilije Vidovic provided me with his whole platoon archive, the complete archive, so we can go through everything, and the fact that many things are lacking there, which I would like to have seen there, what can I do about that? I just want the witness to answer, having looked at this list of 54 men, whether there's a single surname for which he can state it was not from those parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, to save time, you are saying that Vidovic gave you all these documents. Does this mean that you intend to call this person named Vidovic as a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've already used some of Vasilije Vidovic's statements, and he is on my witness list, Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, so a number of issues can be confirmed through this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my question is a very short one, and the witness can give a yes-or-no answer. And if the answer is "yes," then he can tell me which surname is not from those parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you consider, Mr. VS-1055, that on this list of 54 names, there are people there who, judging by their surname, are quite obviously not from those parts; that is to say, Ilijas, Vogosca, Visoko, Breza, up to Zenica and Sarajevo, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have before me page 2. 38, what is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 38 is Faruk Dzafic, son of Mujo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 35 is Ratko -- well, I can't read this. "Zletic," [phoen] is it? I really don't know what that letter is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That man is from Serbia. Ah, it says "Aleksic."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are millions of Aleksics in Bosnia and in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Anyway, the surname is Aleksic. Any other surname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are there no Civcics in those parts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you quite sure there aren't any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Any other doubtful surnames?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Miroslav Krstic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that surname I don't remember having encountered in the Ilijas region. And then there's Radovanovic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No Radovanovics either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know Miroslav Radovanovic from Sarajevo, he was an advisor to Radovan Karadzic and later on a national deputy of the Serbian Radical Party in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you know about that handball player from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew a Radovanovic from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, my chemistry teacher in the first year in Sarajevo was called Milica Radovanovic, so how can you say that there are no surnames of Radovanovic in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, well, you said Bosnia but you asked me about Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I said from Zenica to Sarajevo. Ilijas, Vogosca, Visoko, that general area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gave my answers on that basis, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going too fast. Yes, Mr. Marcussen, did you want to say the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, I just wanted to point out that the witness was not asked about whether these were surnames that were found in Bosnia, but in specific locations, but maybe that was cleared up. It's at page 49, line 2, that the question is found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let's not waste any more time on that. Let's go on through your statement. It's much more reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1055, you stated that after you were taken out, led out of that shelter, one of the men who were with you was wounded, and when Vaske Vidovic and the blonde man appeared, one of them shot that man; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it was Amir Fazlic who was killed in that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then why do you describe it quite differently in your statement? It's page 2 of your statement. Do you have a more legible copy? You say here that when you decided to try to escape, one person managed; two returned, one of them wounded. And then those four allegedly Serbs show up, and then you mention names. In your statement, you say that you were taken back to the shelter again and that this Amir Fazlic was killed in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Amir Fazlic. He was not killed in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Give us a more legible copy, perhaps in the other document. This one was given to the security service, the State Security Service. Do you have a better document? You say here in your statement: "They ordered us to put our heads to the ground and look down, probably so that we can't recognise them. Still, I recognised Vlaja Lizdek, Novo Rasevic, Novo Panjic, and Ranko Draskic. They pushed us into the basement and threatened to liquidate us. There, in the presence of us all, they killed the wounded Amir Fazlic." So you say they pushed you back into the basement and killed Amir Fazlic in the basement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not kill Amir Fazlic in the basement. They killed him outside the basement, while we were still standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they first push you in the basement and then kill him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First they killed Amir while we were still standing, so we were first taken out of the basement, lined us up. They killed him, and then they pushed us back in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you don't mention that Amir was killed by Vaske and his blonde escort; you mention these four men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I failed to mention it, but I said it in the statement given to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the statement given to the Muslim authorities could be false?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe the text is -- the formulations may differ slightly, but the statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So why don't you mention here this man in uniform who came in and introduced himself as an officer of the Seselj guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably didn't make that statement, I didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So when did you remember that officer of the Seselj guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, time does its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you mean the time makes you remember better?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement was given immediately after the traumas that I experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you mean that with the lapse of time, you've started remembering things you didn't remember before, including those things that didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why do you say that Vaske Vidovic drove a white Golf? You say you saw him in a white Golf, and he never drove one, he says.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vaske Vidovic was in a blue --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake, interpreter's correction. It is a blue Golf all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read that it's white, so it's blue, you're quite sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put on the ELMO, please, the statement of Vasilije Vidovic given on the 3rd of June this year. It's very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Here is what Vasilije Vidovic says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, I see what objection you're going to raise. This Vidovic is going to come to -- called to testify, and the accused seemingly has his statement. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I was going to ask the accused to indicate what tab in the binder this comes from so we can follow the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not in the binder and will not be tendered into evidence. You told me yesterday that there is absolutely no need to provide for photocopying the statements that won't be tendered. If you changed your mind again, then I will provide it for photocopying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't wish to have it tendered. You are just showing the document to the witness. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said that I will never again tender anything into evidence, because you refused the documents I offered at the time of Expert Theunens' testimony. I don't think we need raise this issue again. I want to put what Vasilije Vidovic says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. Every time you raise this issue again, the Trial Chamber, when Theunens' testimony was heard, we refused one of the documents. That document posed a problem. We've never denied you any document. We can only admit the document if the document has been translated. If the document is reliable, if the document is relevant and has some probative value, and the document has to be shown to the witness, in that case we admit it. So I would like to correct what you're saying. We have denied you nothing. It is just that when a document is being admitted, it has to meet a number of criteria, and those are the rules I've just set out. In addition, this document, which we are discovering and seeing for the first time, I assume that it has a stamp on it and that certifies the signature. It has not been translated into English, and that is why the Prosecutor is raising a well-substantiated objection. And this document is being used to say, "Well, this is the statement of such-and-such. I'm showing it to you. In this document, the person says this and that in paragraph 2 of page 4, for instance. What do you think of this?" Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, that is the problem, and I apologise that we have to spend time on this, but the fundamental problem here again is that the accused has not respected Your Honours' ruling that he has to notify us, before cross-examination begins, of the documents he intends to use. This is another document that we have not been notified of. This happens repeatedly, and there's no reason why the accused is not complying with Your Honours' guidelines on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this occasion arose yesterday. You may have received it a few minutes ago, but if you'd had the document for a few days already, why wasn't the Prosecutor informed before?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I meant to provide it for copying yesterday, but when you said that there was no need to do that, I didn't provide anything, although I did have another two or three interesting documents. If you are saying now that I should provide it for photocopying earlier, I will do it in the future, but of course a day in advance or an hour in advance, because that's the way I receive these documents. I'm short on time with my preparation for Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, something positive, at least. So photocopy the documents beforehand so that the Prosecutor has it in due time, that the Prosecutor has time to look at it and see what questions can be raised. Every time there is a document you wish to use, ask the usher to photocopy the document and hand it over to the Prosecutor. Then we will have no problem with this. Nonetheless, as you are using this document, put the questions relating to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Vasilije Vidovic puts three main things related to your testimony. Of course, he does not refer to your testimony, itself, but to the certain points you made. He says, in paragraph 1, that the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina found him in his house in Ilijas; that Serbs there, educated by their -- informed by the experience of Serbs in surrounding places, self-organised in order to protect themselves, he says. He had with him his relatives, friends and neighbours from Ilijas. There were also Serbs who had fled from Zenica, and that in his unit there were no outside volunteers from the territory of another republic or anybody speaking in the Ekavian dialect of Serbia proper. He says the only person who spoke the Ekavian dialect of Serbia proper was my "kum," Vladimir Dobricic, a reporter of the Danube News Agency. Now, he was the commander of the unit who was always officially called "Vaske's Platoon," as he says, or is the truth what you remembered subsequently and you couldn't remember in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Vaske's writing is a blatant lie. He will probably have the opportunity to come to this Court, and I volunteer to confront him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the witness, does he have the right to call somebody a liar, to call something a lie? On the contrary, I believe the Defence has some latitude in cross-examination. However, I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Vasilije Vidovic goes on to say: "If somebody claims that in my unit there were volunteers from outside speaking in Ekavian dialect or that I had brought some people from the battlefield in Benkovac, where I had been earlier, then that person does not know me or has never seen me during the armed conflicts." Is this true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vaske Vidovic and I know each other very well, and it's not true, what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When were you born, which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is Vaske older?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's perhaps three or four years my senior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it says "two years" here, but it doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It really doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why did you lie that Vaske Vidovic was wearing glasses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Here's what he says here: "Anyone who claims that I had in my units volunteers from Benkovac --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Here we go again. It is not professional of you to continue characterising the witness as a liar, unless you're able to prove that he is deliberately lying. He may be mistaken about the fact of whether a person was wearing glasses or not, but that is not tantamount to lying. The same goes for the witness. The witness should also refrain from characterising people who are not present in this courtroom as liars. Is this clear to both of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question to put to the witness concerning the glasses. Maybe I misunderstood yesterday. I had understood yesterday that you said he didn't really need the glasses, he was just wearing them to pass himself off as somebody else. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Vaske Vidovic says about this: "Anyone who claims that I had volunteers from Benkovac in my unit is telling a complete untruth, just as anyone who claims that I wear glasses for my sight. I've never worn glasses to improve my vision, just as I don't wear them today at the age of 54." You claim this is not true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim this is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. As regards the glasses, yesterday you said that he wore glasses, but were these sunglasses or proper glasses, because you can wear sunglasses without needing reading glasses which you are wearing at the moment. When you talked about the glasses, which glasses did you mean; did you mean sunglasses or reading glasses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The glasses were like those worn by Draza Mihajlovic, identical, so he was impersonating Draza Mihajlovic. It may have been a negligible dioptre, but he did wear them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Draza Mihajlovic had reading glasses or sunglasses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For his sight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were white lenses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the Muslims of Ilijas who had already been working on the police force were called upon to continue working in the police of SAO Romanija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that since they refused, a peaceful division of the police force was agreed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then you probably don't know that the weaponry, communications equipment and vehicles were divided equally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some weapons were distributed. I spoke about it a little yesterday. About equipment and cars, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where Ljubina village is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubina village, we call it the upper parts, is towards Srednje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When the police force was divided, is it the case that the Muslims organised new premises of their force in the primary school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Ljubina is between 15 and 17 kilometres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But Ljesevo, Misoca, Luka and Ljubina were covered by this new police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did these Muslim policemen ever appear in Ljesevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communication was impossible if -- once Ilijas was occupied by the Serb police after this division.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what was the official name of Vaske's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have here another statement by General Josipovic, and I'm going to use it in the cross-examination of the forthcoming witnesses. He says that the real name of the unit, Vaske's unit, was the Motorised Platoon of the Assault Battalion, and he confirms that the military post number of that unit was 7491/17. Could that be correct, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date of that statement of the general's?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The 3rd of June, 2008.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The statement was given for the purposes of this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Josipovic would not have given that statement in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what would he have said in June 1992? Go on, then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he would have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How could you say that General Josipovic was the commander of the garrison in Visoko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I knew that he was the commander in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Dragan Josipovic was never the commander of the garrison in Visoko, nor was he in Visoko at all. Dragan Josipovic, in June 1992, came from the 36th Mechanised Brigade from Subotica to Han Pijesak and was deployed there in the Ilijas Brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Josipovic was the commander of the barracks in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Josipovic claims he was never in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that can be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, yes, and I suppose that the Prosecution will establish that because you're a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said during the examination-in-chief that the brother-in-law of Fazlic was a relative of Moammar el-Gadhafi and that his surname was Gadhafi too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, to avoid wasting any time and a lot of confusion, a while ago Mr. Seselj talked about a document that came from Josipovic. He said that Vaske and other men belonged to the unit numbered 7491-17, which would tend to mean that these men belonged to a military unit. So I went to check Mr. Seselj's document instantly, those documents which are in his binders, and since I react very promptly, I can see that Andric, Nadan, one of the soldiers, is mentioned as belonging to this unit, 7491-17, who seemingly, on the 13th of December, 1992, was wounded in a settlement called Golo Brdo Dzukija [phoen]. So this document establishes that there was a military unit in 1992. So much for this. Does it change anything to the answers you will give to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should look at the date when that unit was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's another question altogether. But Vaske's unit may be seen as an official unit that reported to the VRS, since we have an official number for this unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might have become an official unit at some point. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I just wanted to mention this. Mr. Seselj, it seems that as far as the remaining time still allotted to you, you would have 30 minutes left, normally speaking. We have spent 21 minutes discussing the documents because there were a series of objections. Theoretically, that time is taken off your time, so you would have nine minutes left. Since we are not too pressed for time today, I want to mention this. You have 20 or so minutes left, and use them purposefully, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite clear, Mr. President, how it is that you can deduct that procedural discussion about documents from my time. That procedural discussion was opened by the Prosecutor, and if that was not in order, then you should deduct it from his time. All you should count is the effective time I took in cross-examining the Prosecution witness. Everything else is deducted from other people's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, submissions on a document presented during cross-examination, when questions are put to a witness, this is not the right procedure. This has to do with the merits of the case, and we are not talking about procedural matters here. This is a matter of some substance. When you show a document, you should anticipate the Prosecutor's objections, if any. You should bear all of this in mind, because if there is an objection, normally speaking, your time is numbered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, how then -- what happens when the Prosecutor produces documents during the examination-in-chief and I make my observations and objections; how is that time not deducted from the Prosecution time? He's given a total number of hours or time, whereas different criteria are being applied to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... you challenge this document, there is an exchange of views, and if you challenge it, too bad for the Prosecution. But if your objection is unfounded, then there's no reason why the Prosecutor should be prejudiced. So in this particular instance, Mr. Marcussen's remarks on these documents were founded, well founded, since he reminded us that there is a procedure relating to the disclosure of exhibits in English. This is what I had to say to you. Please proceed now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I'm not going to make any more comments, or objections, or present any more documents. I will behave in line with your increasing restrictions, because if I have to be anxious over whether the Prosecutor will intervene during my time and then spend that time of mine, then there's no sense to that. You've introduced all sorts of rules that never existed in this Tribunal, where many rules like that did exist, but you can do what you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I asked the question, and you said that the brother-in-law of Vasilije Vidovic was a distant relation of Moammar el-Gadhafi and that his surname was Gadhafi, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that, and that was the rumour going 'round the entire municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you don't know that for a fact, but you heard the rumours going 'round?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that his surname was Gadhafi, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And so having heard that somewhere, you're presenting that as a fact, as the truth here, are you? And I put it to you now that the brother-in-law of Vasilije Vidovic was called Abdul Salaam Salas [phoen] and that he was no relation to the Libyan President Gadhafi at all. So who's right, you on the basis of the rumours you heard, or I, who have the information at hand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're right, there's no problem there, but that doesn't change the facts, the situation, the fact of why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it does, and you'll see how it does just now. Abdul Salaam Salas for years was in the diplomatic mission of Libya in Belgrade. He was an officer of the Libyan army. And the sister of Vasilije Vidovic is married to this man. As a Serbian woman of the Orthodox faith, she converted to the Islamic faith, and Vaske's nephews are Muslims. And I met his sister and his brother-in-law, and we were on very friendly terms in Belgrade. Now, you take this same man, Vaske, who had no prejudices at all, his sister having married a Muslim, a Muslim from an orthodox Islamic state such as Libya, to boot, who observes all the religious rites of his faith and whose nephews are Muslims, you accuse him of destroying the mosques of Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Vidovic, Vasilije Vidovic, as far as I heard, did destroy Ilijas' mosque, and against his brother-in-law, his sister and nephews, I have absolutely nothing against them and wish them all the best in life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But I have a document here which was issued by the [indiscernible] of the Islamic community of Sarajevo in which it states that at the end of 1992, the mosque in Ilijas was destroyed. And at that time when the Ilijas mosque was destroyed, Vaske Vidovic and his platoon were at the front, at the Nisic Plateau, where they were sent as reinforcements to the Serb forces there facing the Muslim onslaught in that part of the country. So Vaske Vidovic and his unit weren't in Ilijas at all when the mosque was destroyed, and you are accusing him of having destroyed the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that Vasilije Vidovic had destroyed not only the mosque in Ilijas but also all the mosques which existed in Ilijas municipality, that is to say, Ljesevo, Visoca [phoen], and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who did you get that from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from people who came from Ilijas after the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of the people you heard this from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Go on, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, sir. You've been granted protective measures. If you give someone's name, a smart journalist will be quick to identify this person and ask who might have said that, and in that case your name would be mentioned. Let's redact line 7, page 66. Let's move into private session so that you can give these names. Registrar, can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to The Hague Tribunal investigators in 2004, you acknowledged the fact that a division did take place, that is to say, that the Muslim and Serb police separated, whereas a moment ago you denied any knowledge of that separation. In paragraph 12, in fact, you state the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Mr. Seselj is moving on to another topic. The question relating to the mosques is an important one. Witness, you said that you heard rumours to the effect that Vaske had destroyed some mosques; amongst others, one in Ilijas. It so happens that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment. Let me finish. It so happens that Mr. Seselj has proof of this. I don't know. He seems to be saying that according to his evidence, Vaske and his unit were elsewhere. Therefore, if they were elsewhere, it is difficult to understand how they would have destroyed the mosque. But in addition, the accused seems to have a letter provided by the Islamic Community, to the effect that the mosque was destroyed at the end of December, from what I understood, and not in June. And in December, Vaske is no longer there, he's on the front line, he's elsewhere. So those people who told you that, were they 100 per cent sure about this, did they just convey the rumours they'd heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no mention of the date here when the mosque was destroyed. In talking to people, when we spoke about the suffering of both sides, I asked specifically why the mosques, and then they said, "Vaske did that with his men."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no letter from the Islamic religious community. All I have is an excerpt from one of their publications, "The Medzlis of the Islamic Community in Sarajevo," and the portion related to Ilijas Dzemat District, where it says that the mosque was destroyed, as they say, at the end of 1992, using the word "Konac." And that in 1996, it was reconstructed with the help of the Egyptian government and that the people now refer to it as the Egyptian mosque. So I have no letter, I just have the photocopy of part of the publication, but what was important to me was the date of the mosque destruction, and I have information from Vasilije Vidovic himself that at that time he was at the Nisic Plateau with his unit. That's the essence of my question on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has answered the question. Please continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 12 of the statement to The Hague Tribunal, you said -- allegedly said the following: "When the Serbs formed their own police force in Ilijas, the Muslims and Croats decided to do the same, and the police station was to be located in Ljesevo. At the time of the split, the Serb police had given us Muslims and Croats half of the ammunitions they had. Contrary to the Serb police, we were not organised at all. We didn't know who to put in charge, what to do in case of attack, et cetera. We decided that our police commander was to be Omer Spahic, who lived in Ilijas. We told him over the phone about all the problems we had, like not having enough staff to do the job, what to do in case of an attack, et cetera." That means that you knew that the police force had been split, you knew that a Muslim police force had been established, and that the commander of the police force was Omer Spahic, and you said "we decided," so you took part in that. And a moment ago in the cross-examination, you said you had no idea about any of that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not have any idea about all that, and when I said that, I wasn't speaking in my own name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the question that was put to the witness was whether or not he was aware that the Muslims had been -- the Muslim policemen had been invited or asked to be part of the SAO Romanija police force and thereafter had left, and the witness said that he did not know about that. He did not say that he did not know about the split in the police, and he testified during direct examination to this yesterday, so it's a mischaracterisation of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything Mr. Marcussen said is not true. Please, look at the transcript and you will see. It was the initial question in that set of questions that was followed by the question if he knows that the police was divided, where the headquarters of the police were. He even said that not a single Muslim policeman appeared in Ljesevo. He said it in front of you people 15, 20 minutes ago. Do you remember that detail when I asked him if a single Muslim policeman appeared in Ljesevo? He said he had never seen any. What is the Prosecutor doing, and how come you tolerate it all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not tolerating anything. We are listening to your question, we are listening to the Prosecutor's objection. When the Prosecution asks questions, you also raise objections, and we listen to everything. We're not here to tolerate anything. Reformulate your question, please, so we can understand whether there is a problem or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why would I formulate my question, I wonder. I mean "reformulate my question." My question was clear. I caught the witness in a contradiction. I showed him his own statement from 1994. He doesn't confirm what he was saying. He denied it all here. He said he knew nothing about that Muslim police, he never saw a single Muslim policeman in Ljesevo after the division. Why should I reformulate anything. I won't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj asked me, if I remember correctly, about the police in Ljubina, which was 15, 17 kilometres away from me, and about them I said I knew nothing, and I really know nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was whether he had ever seen a Muslim policeman in Ljesevo, a policeman of the Muslim police force after the division.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police in Ljesevo, after the division, did not operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why are you complaining to The Hague investigators here that, unlike the Serbian police -- unlike the Serb police, you were not organised at all, you didn't even know who to appoint as commander, and then you say, "We decided that our police commander should be Omer Spahic from Ilijas?" Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible to form the police right there, right then, and Omer Spahic, from the police force you are mentioning, is from Ljubina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you decided he should be your commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but active in the area of Ljubina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, your time is -- you've already used two hours. Your time is up, your cross-examination is over. If you have one last question, put your last questions quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to ask any more questions, and I will think about whether I'm going to ask any questions of future witnesses. It's my entitlement to decide not to conduct any cross-examination at all. I'll think it over during the weekend, because this has already turned into some sort of mis-treatment and some kind of terror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give you my answer later, but after the witness left the courtroom. Mr. Marcussen, any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, then, on behalf of my fellow Judges and myself, I'd like to thank you for having come to testify for the Prosecution. I wish you all the best, and I wish you a safe return home. I will now ask the usher to please escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I told you that I was going to answer what you just said. You are entitled to ask questions during the cross-examination, which is what you did during the time that was allotted to you. The Prosecutor had two hours and you also had two hours, so you had the same amount of time. Therefore, there's no problem here. Secondly, during the questions you asked, the Prosecution raised a number of objections linked to the fact that they were given the documents at the very last minute or not even given the documents at all. You gave us your reasons for this. I'll give you credit for it. It is true that if you obtain yourself a document at the last minute, it is quite normal that you can't give it ahead of time to the Prosecution. Yesterday, you said at one point in time you wanted to make photocopies and there was a problem, the photocopies could not be made. Very well, we will try to do better next time. We are trying to solve problems as they come up, and in the interests of all, of course, and in the interests of yourself also. The Trial Chamber knows that you have some material problems to defend yourself; you're alone, you don't have an entire staff there to make photocopies for you in realtime, whereas the OTP does. We know this and we take this into account, which is why sometimes we allow you to do a number of things that we would never allow elsewhere, because we do take this into account, the fact that you are representing yourself. However, this being said, how are you mistreated so far regarding your case, when you were trying to challenge the reliability of witnesses or the merits of their testimony? We let you -- you were very free to ask all questions you wanted to ask, and sometimes the Trial Chamber also picked up on a number of issues that you might have neglected and asked questions. So what you said earlier surprises me. I don't quite understand why you're complaining, but I will give you the floor. But, please, tell us what your problems are, but very calmly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am always, constantly, composed and calm. You have told me now for the first time, although we are six or eight months into the trial, that all the time used by the Prosecutor to present justifiable objections is taken from my cross-examination time. You have directly infringed upon my right to due process. Nothing the Prosecutor says can be taken away from my time. But since you have made that decision, then I have very calmly, very rationally, in a very composed manner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Maybe you have not understood me correctly, and if there's a misunderstanding, let's get to the bottom of things immediately. I believe that a few days ago -- a few weeks ago, actually, the Trial Chamber issued an oral decision regarding the time allotted to the parties when far-fetched objections were raised. I don't have it here, but I'm sure the legal officer will help me find it. But we said that when there were objections that were not grounded, then the time spent on this objection would be taken out of the one who raised this unfounded objection in the first place. Why is that? Very simple. Just imagine a situation where either the Prosecution or yourself would just stand up all the time and raise objections, totally ungrounded with no reasons whatsoever, and then the other party would have to answer, the Judges would have to rule on the objection. This could be a huge waste of time, which is why we issued this oral decision drawing everybody's attention on the problem. There are objections raised by the Prosecutor which are grounded and there are objections which you raise that are also grounded, but sometimes the Prosecutor raised ungrounded objections and sometimes you did the same. I don't have the list here with me, but this is all I wanted to say. I don't want any misunderstanding on this issue. Furthermore, earlier I was told that the time spent on objections amounted to 21 minutes. I kept you abreast of this, I told you about this. I told you that theoretically this time should be deducted from your own time, but I told you it won't be deducted and I'll give you an extra -- you'll still have 20 minutes. So I did not deduct anything from you. I even said that we had some time and we were not pressed for time, so we were not going to look at the watch that closely. I did not, therefore, sort your objections to put on the one hand the grounded ones and, on the other hand, the ungrounded ones. It is true that sometimes you make well-grounded objections and they're sustained, and sometimes you don't and we tell you about it, but the same applies to the Prosecutor, and sometimes he's not too happy with it, but he knows exactly what the Rules are. Maybe there is a misunderstanding in what I had said earlier, but I want to say that today no time was deducted from your time regarding objections. You used up all of your two hours. Did you get -- did you understand this or do you want me to expound on this? I don't want any misunderstanding between the Trial Chamber and yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have three things to tell you, if you insist. First of all, in my assessment, I did not use two full hours. Second, the first decision you made is discriminatory. It applies only to me. If I make unjustified objections in cross-examination, I bear the consequences, but if the Prosecutor makes unfounded objections during cross-examination, he bears no consequences. And, third, today for the first time you put forth this theory that whenever I show a document here and the Prosecutor objects, if the objection is justified, all the procedural discussion about that document is theoretically, as you put it, deducted from my time. This is the first time I hear of such a theory. Even in cross-examination, if I raise procedural issues or I address the Trial Chamber, even that should not count against my time. Why don't you look who, in these past eight months, made more relevant comments, the Prosecutor or I. I guarantee to you that three-fourths of my comments were certainly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I have the oral decision here on the screen, and let me read to you two of the "noting." "Noting that at this stage of the procedure, the Trial Chamber notes the very important time spent by the accused for submissions during the examination-in-chief, whereas these submissions should be made during the cross-examination; noting that fairness of the proceedings require that when such interventions are made this time should be deducted from the time allocated to the accused for his cross-examination." So this decision was aimed at your interventions during the examination-in-chief, but there could be exactly the opposite also. There could be the same kind of interventions from the Prosecution during the cross-examination, submissions that would be made or interventions that would be made without any grounds, and because of fairness, of course, we need to have -- to do the same thing regarding time for both parties, you're absolutely right, because it's during the cross-examination, if the Prosecutor is making an objection that is overruled, this time is not deducted from my time. It is true that it is a problem that does exist, and there is no solution right now to it. The Trial Chamber has not discussed this, and it's true that you have raised a real problem here, but in the future you could always make a comment once, twice, or three times to the Prosecutor, saying that he's making a mistake and it's ungrounded, but it's true that if he continues, there could be sanctions handed down. So this is what I want to say. When you have two hours for your cross-examination, the Trial Chamber would like this time to be spent wisely and purposefully. When the Prosecutor raises his objection, we do not want him to make you -- put you off track. If the Prosecution makes ungrounded objections, of course he will be sanctioned. But if, at the same time, you're also dealing with other problems, for example, that have to do with a document, this is what happened now, you just showed a document to the witness, the Prosecutor raised an objection and you said, "This is procedure," and I said, "No, this is the merits," because normally, according to the Rules, the document should have been disclosed to the Prosecution and should have been translated in one of the working languages of the Tribunal, which was not the case regarding this document. So the time spent on this document is to be blamed on you. It's because of you that all this time was wasted. It's not the Trial Chamber's fault or the Prosecution's, because you did not play by the Rule there. Now, you told us why you didn't do this. You gave us your explanation, and we accepted your explanation. But just imagine, if you don't abide by the Rules, if you continue giving us documents that are not translated, that were not disclosed to the Prosecution, if you've had these documents for quite a while, of course the Prosecution is going to rise to its feet and is going to raise objections, and we waste time, which is why the Trial Chamber asks you to do your utmost to make sure these documents be disclosed in time to the Prosecution. You undertook to do this. We will have photocopies, then, and if possible we would also like to have translations. And I noted, and I want to congratulate you for this, you know, in the three binders you gave us, Mr. Vaske Vidovic's notebook regarding this period of reference was translated into English. Thank you. Then there's no problem. You can ask for all the documents who are translated to be admitted, and you can tender them if you want, but I don't want any misunderstanding between us. You did raise a problem, there is a problem, and I don't have a solution yet. It is true that if the Prosecution is wasting time, I don't really know what the solution could be yet. Remember that this goes both ways, anyway. The decision that was issued is applied to the two parties. If the Prosecution is deliberately wasting time, he will be sanctioned. This works both ways. These procedural matters are extremely tedious and are taking up a lot of time. I would like us to spend all the time we have listening to witnesses, looking at the documents, listening to your questions, listening to the Prosecution's questions, rather than spending time and hours and hours on procedural matters, because in the end the judgement will not be rendered on procedural matters, it will be rendered on the merits of the case, on documents, on statements, on questions and on answers, not on the fact, you know, that such-and-such party was deducted a couple of minutes here or there. This is all I had to say to Mr. Seselj. Rest assured, Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber never intended to limit your Defence. You have the right to ask questions. You take advantage of this right, of course, but in order to use this rightfully, the right logistics need to be in place. We need to have the documents, and when we have a text shown to us in Serbian, we should have a translation so we can know what's in the text. Otherwise, we have to trust you blindly, and so does the Prosecution, because they don't have the translation either. And like the witness said very justly, "It is true that I have this paragraph, but I would like to read the rest of the book to know the rest of the story." But we couldn't do this because, in the first place, we didn't have the book and we didn't have the other pages. So as you see, there are some problems here. It's true that when you -- a person representing himself in this situation, there are material problems that crop up, but I think they can be solved if everyone is ready to do so. Do you want to take the floor again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, you've put some things upside down, topsy-turvy. The witness said here that he read, in the book "Ilijaski Nemanjici" by author Adzic, that Vaske Vidovic organised the transport of oil and fuel from the military depot to Knin, and you should have asked the Prosecutor where that book was, because the witness relates to this written source. The Prosecutor examined the witness, and in 2004 he held proofing sessions, so the Prosecutor knew that the witness would state this, so why didn't you ask to see the book, where the book is? I managed to find the book between yesterday and today, and this morning, by fax I was sent five or six pages from the book, and now it seems the problem is on my side for not providing the whole book. The whole book deals with the war, not just this oil transport by train. That's only mentioned on one page in the book -- of the book. And now you said the witness said that correctly, and can I see the whole book? Well, it's just one train load. One barrel doesn't make the entire book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor to Mr. Marcussen. But what you're telling us regarding this book, you are well aware that Judges do not know what the Prosecution disclosed to you, we don't know what the contents of this is. So since we didn't know this, we could have thought that this book had been disclosed by the Prosecutor to yourself, so both parties knew the content of the book and the Judges knew nothing about it. This is what came to my mind at first. And then also I said that maybe the person involved had read the book without telling the Prosecution about it, about having read this book. But since you had a document on this matter of fuel transport which seemed to go again -- which seemed to be in favour of what the witness was saying, I didn't decide to go into that because obviously with the book, there seemed to be elements that were contradicting what the witness was saying. But then you say, "Why didn't you ask for the book to be produced, given or presented?" First, I didn't ask for that because I didn't know whether the book had been disclosed or not, and the only thing interesting here was on the fuel transport. And according to the pages we saw, it does seem that the unit in charge was not Vaske's unit, so there was no need to talk about all this. Mr. Marcussen, maybe you wanted to take the floor on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I just wanted to point out that I did not object to the use of this document, so the arguments are irrelevant. Your Honours are talking about other objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now this issue of the book is over now. Mr. Seselj would like to say something else?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned what we wasted time over. Well, precisely over the comments made by the Prosecutor with respect to the translated document, the document that was handed over in December. I think it says here when the document was submitted for translation, and it has indeed been translated into English. So that's what the discussion was about, and now the Prosecutor made the objection that in several places in the document, dates are mentioned from 1994 and 1995. That's what the debate was about, and you said that that debate should be theoretically deducted from my time. I don't know what theory that is, but, anyway, everything was translated and prepared in advance, and the Prosecutor received a well-ordered binder and list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, as far as I understand the rules that we have been applying so far, the general rule is that time spent on discussion of documents brought by a party is deducted from that party's time. This is, I think, a very natural rule of criminal procedure, and the only issue, therefore, remains to determine whether the objections raised by the Prosecution, in relation to the documents that you brought, should perhaps be characterized instead as a discussion on procedural matters. Now, I don't think that this would be appropriate in this case, because the discussion we had was about the authenticity and the correct construction of Vidovic's book, but, nevertheless, the Presiding Judge decided not to deduct the time we spent on that. So you were given the full two hours, and so I think although there may be some complaint in the end, you suffered no prejudice, you suffered no harm in your right to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim that never, up 'til now, a second of the Prosecutor's time was deducted that we spent discussing my appropriate or inappropriate objections and comments to the way in which the examination-in-chief was being conducted or documents presented, never a single second. You're now telling me about a new rule, it seems, a rule that never existed. So far what happened was this: The Prosecutor's time was counted -- just the effective time of examination-in-chief of the witness was counted. Even the time when the -- the time it took to place the document on the screen was deducted -- or, rather, was not counted as being his time, the Prosecution's time. Now you're telling me of a new rule, it seems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I think we need to check the transcripts. I can't say whether you are right or wrong, but empirically speaking, I have the feeling that when the witness -- when the Prosecution calls a witness and shows documents to this witness, you object and say, "Well, there's this and that in the document." I have the feeling that while you are making your comments, this time is taken off the Prosecution's time. I might be wrong. The Registrar can tell us what the case is. I have the feeling that oftentimes this is taken off the Prosecution's time. We can improve on this system, of course. I'm not saying that we have the best system in the world. The system can be improved upon with the help of your comments. And I don't have the feeling, and this was said by my colleagues a while ago, that the Prosecution, or you, for that matter, have suffered from your time being narrowed down. I stand to be corrected, but for the time being, I don't think you have been prejudiced in any way. Now, in addition, Mr. Seselj, imagine you are to address an important issue. The Judges will take it off their time when they want to put questions, so rest assured, if you address a crucial issue, you must know that the Bench will put questions and that no time will be taken off if there are objections. What we are interested in is getting to the truth, and getting to the truth means sometimes that one has to accept a number of constraints, i.e., not always watch the clock. But we need to have rules also. Since we need rules, let me specify that we will hear two witnesses next week who have been scheduled. The first witness has not been granted any protective measures; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. There will be an application for protective measures, so I just wanted to make sure that the name is not being mentioned today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall not quote any names. We will be hearing two witnesses, and I shall not give any names. According to our schedule, the first witness will be heard for two hours, the second also, and so the Prosecution will have two hours and the accused will have two hours. The first witness will come back on the next day. When we have finished with the first witness, we will hear the second witness. This is what has been planned. Now, as far as protective measures are concerned, you are going to be applying, in writing, I assume, for protective measures, or are you going to apply for these protective measures now, orally? In that case, we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, a motion might already have been filed. I'm unsure what has been done this morning. I'm at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We could make an oral application, I guess, but I would just need five minutes to consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please. You will have the floor. Just wait to hear what he is about to say, because I'm like you, I am just finding it out now. So there is a written motion that has been filed, that we don't have, but you can still --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I will give you the floor, but let me just specify that when an issue relating to protective measures is mentioned at the last minute, the Trial Chamber, and this is something I've done in previous cases, when last-minute events arise, the blinds are then dropped. The witness comes into the courtroom. We put questions to the witness. You have the floor, the Prosecutor has the floor, and the Trial Chamber settles the matter one way or another. We don't know. This can happen. In certain cases, during the proofing session the witness says something which changes the situation. In that case, the Trial Chamber needs to apply this procedure at the last minute. This is what can happen sometimes in the best of cases. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, more and more improbable things are happening here. Yesterday, we heard a case where the witness waited in front of the courtroom while we were discussing the introduction of protective measures. The motion was filed by the Prosecution on the 30th of May, and it was handed -- or, rather, the translation of it was handed to me the day before yesterday. So it was the day before yesterday I learned about it, and I raised the issue yesterday, and I waived my right to those seven days in which I could have stated my views. I could have said yesterday, "It is my right to think about this matter for seven days," and then respond. So I waived that right of mine. Then the right that I had to appeal within seven days, you curtailed it to just one day, reduced it to just one day, so I could have done that until 8.30 last night, for instance. And, of course, I didn't do that because I had more important things to do rather than writing that request, because I thought in advance that you would reject it. Now, today you are allowing the Prosecutor to say that, "The witness which has been announced for next week is not a protected witness, but we are preparing a written motion for protective measures to be put in place." Now, if the Prosecutor is preparing a motion, he might file it tomorrow. When is that motion going to be translated into Serbian when we have the weekend coming up? So I would have this in Serbian on Monday, perhaps, if they work over the weekend, and then I promise that I'll keep quiet, wait for the seven-day deadline, and then I'll appeal and write my response, and then you won't be able to hear the witness on Tuesday. Otherwise, the Prosecutor will have to table two motions, one motion to enforce protective measures five years after the witness was placed on the witness list, and the second request, that the Trial Chamber should urgently make a new ruling whereby my right to respond within seven days is reduced to the right to, let's say, 15 minutes. I propose you just give me 15 minutes to state my views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are giving me the opportunity to discuss it. I reflected on it during the night. First of all, the Prosecution calls witnesses to testify. The Prosecutor needs to tell the witness that there will be a proofing session, and the witness might be coming on a Saturday. This is a working assumption. And then at the last minute the witness will tell the Prosecution this and that happened. What does the Prosecution do in that case? The Prosecution files a motion in writing, if he has the time to do so. Otherwise, at the start of the hearing the Prosecution will say that it needs protective measures. This can happen. This is a real-life situation. This can happen to you also. Maybe a witness will say to you, "I have a problem and I need protective measures," and he tells you this at the last minute. So at the last minute, you will do the same thing. That is my first answer. My second: As far as protective measures are concerned, Rule 75 is designed for this particular situation. Rule 75 specifies this, and I shall read it out as follows so that you understand the system well: "A Judge or Chamber may, proprio motu, or at the request of either party ..." Which means that a Trial Chamber, irrespective of what the Prosecution may think or what you may think, can decide to grant protective measures, and there is no need to ask either party's opinion. Proprio motu, the Trial Chamber can grant protective measures. This means that when a witness is waiting in the parlour and when in the courtroom we say that the blinds need to be dropped, to my mind this has to do with a discretion of the Trial Chamber, irrespective of the Prosecution or the Defence's opinion. That is a first working assumption. The second would be that the Trial Chamber knows nothing about anything at all. The Prosecution and the Defence both file a motion in writing. This is the purpose of Rule 75. Otherwise, Rule 75 would have stated that a Trial Chamber can, after having obtained information from the Prosecution and from the Defence, grant these measures. This is not mentioned in the Rule in question. The Rules of Procedure is designed to ensure protection, and we bear the parties in mind. Don't forget one thing, Mr. Seselj. The protective measures are granted not in favour of the Prosecution or of the Defence, for that matter. The measures are granted in the interest of the witness. It is for the witness to ask for these protective measures. It is not for the Prosecution to initiate this request, but in certain cases the Prosecution feels that this is not a problem, the person -- and the witness feels that this is not an issue, but the Trial Chamber feels that this is an issue and can, proprio motu, grant these protective measures. This is all enshrined in Rule 75. Read this Rule again. Rule 75 addresses the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, but first and foremost the witness, who is at the center of this. I don't know if you'd like to take the floor again. Otherwise, we will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber really has enormous powers, but those powers it is duty-bound to use in the interests of justice. The trend that obviously exists now is that almost all witnesses who appear in this trial will be testifying secretly under a pseudonym. Now, we had cases here of witnesses who had protective measures put in place until they appeared in the courtroom, and then it turned out that nobody ever asked them whether they wanted protective measures or not, but the Prosecution introduced this of its own. We had cases of that kind, too. Then there were cases of witnesses who showed here the motives that they were falsely testifying about and the privileges they enjoy for giving false testimony. I don't want to mention the names of those witnesses or their pseudonyms. And now we have a new trend, that every next person coming in should enjoy protective measures in this courtroom. Something always happens, something always turns up, and what it is, we see actually trivialities. Nobody is in any danger, or threatened in any way, or in jeopardy, or can have any negative repercussions, so don't keep saying, as you've done in the past, that I will have that same right. Nobody can be a Defence witness who does not have the integrity to say, "I wish to testify about everything publicly, in open session, I wish to tell the truth, regardless of where that will lead me and what will happen." Those are the kind of Defence witnesses that I intend to bring in here. Anybody ashamed to testify or anybody frightened of testifying cannot be a Defence witness, cannot be one of my witnesses. Now, how you're going to act, given that situation, what you're going to do is, once again, your own affair. The Prosecution seems not to be able to find its way. It's running around like a blind chicken in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects to any kind of suggestion that witnesses have been false witnesses or false testimony has been given, particularly with respect to those witnesses for whom protective measures were granted. It is outrageous for the accused to come into this room and argue that the very witnesses who are the most vulnerable and those for whom the Trial Chamber has issued protective measures gave false testimony. That is a very, very dangerous thing for the accused to say, and with all due respect, Your Honours, I think it's time for us to break for the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber on several occasions has told you, as Mr. Mundis has just said, not to say this. When I give you the floor, I cannot put Scotch tape on your mouth, I can't do that, and you take the floor. You have been warned on several occasions. The witnesses take the solemn declaration. They testify. You put questions to them, you can highlight a number of contradictions, failings, lies in certain cases, that's your job as part of the cross-examination, and the Trial Chamber will draw its own conclusions. However -- and you are quite right, protective measures shouldn't be granted to all and everyone. You know this full well. You know that the Prosecution had filed applications to be given granted protective measures for some of its witnesses. In certain cases, these measures were granted; in others, not. The Trial Chamber is guided by the sole protection of the witness if these fears are justified. This is the way we work. We decide in light of the submissions of the Prosecution and your submission. Once again, on behalf of my colleagues who've told you this many a time, stop saying that we are in the presence of false witnesses or the upcoming witnesses will be false witnesses. We do not know anything about this. It is only right at the end that we will know. The Registrar is looking at me because the tapes have stopped. We shall meet again on Tuesday, and we will begin at a quarter past 2.00. Thank you.
